nodes.title: Compute services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: 'Compute' is everything that runs your code: VMs, containers, serverless functions, batch jobs. The exam wants you to pick the right shape — long-running stateful workload → VM, packaged app → container, event-driven short job → serverless.

flashcards.front: VM vs container vs serverless — pick a service for each.
flashcards.back: VM (EC2 / Compute Engine / Azure VM) when you need full OS control. Container (ECS, GKE, AKS, Cloud Run) when you've packaged an app and want orchestration. Serverless (Lambda, Functions, Cloud Functions) for short event-driven tasks, no infrastructure to manage.

A service that adds/removes compute instances based on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, custom metric). Scale-out is cheap; scale-in saves money. Target tracking is the simplest mode: 'keep average CPU at 60%'.

flashcards.front: Spot / preemptible / low-priority — what's the catch?
flashcards.back: Up to 90% off list price, but the cloud can yank the instance with 30 s – 2 min warning. Use for fault-tolerant batch jobs, CI runners, big-data clusters. Don't use for stateful databases or anything that needs to stay up.
On-demand: pay by the hour or second, no commitment. Reserved / committed: 1-3 year commitment, 30-60% discount, no flexibility. Pick reserved for steady baseline load, on-demand for spiky workloads.

nodes.title: Observability and monitoring: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Observability is metrics + logs + traces — the three pillars. You need all three to debug a production incident: metrics tell you something is wrong, logs tell you what happened, traces tell you where in the call graph the problem lives.

flashcards.front: Metrics vs logs vs traces — what does each tell you?
flashcards.back: Metrics: numeric time-series, cheap to store, perfect for dashboards and alerts ('p99 latency = 800 ms'). Logs: discrete events with context, expensive at scale, perfect for forensics. Traces: causally-linked spans showing a request's full path through services.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between an alert and a notification?
flashcards.back: An alert is a condition that fires when a metric crosses a threshold (CPU > 80% for 5 min). The notification is the resulting message (email, Slack, PagerDuty page). One alert can fan out to many notifications. Tuning alerts is harder than wiring notifications.

flashcards.front: What is an SLI / SLO / SLA?
flashcards.back: SLI (indicator): the metric you actually measure ('% of requests under 200 ms'). SLO (objective): the internal target ('99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 28 days'). SLA (agreement): the contractual promise to customers, usually weaker than the SLO so you have buffer.

Plain-text logs are unparseable at scale. Structured logs (JSON, with timestamp + level + service + request_id + key fields) are indexable, queryable, and join-able across services. Most platforms auto-extract fields from JSON without configuration.

questions.q: A Databricks SQL warehouse powers a set of dashboards that are only used between 09:00 and 18:00. The team wants to keep costs down without breaking dashboard responsiveness during the day. Which single configuration change is the most cost-effective and preserves usability?
choices: Enable auto-stop with a short idle timeout (for example, 10 minutes).
Set the minimum and maximum cluster size to the largest tier and disable auto-stop.
Move the workload to an all-purpose cluster shared with the ML team.
Delete the warehouse every evening and recreate it each morning by hand.
questions.explanation: Enabling auto-stop with a short idle window lets the warehouse spin down automatically after quiet periods (nights, weekends, lunch) while remaining available on demand during business hours. Disabling auto-stop bills the largest tier 24/7. All-purpose clusters use a higher DBU rate for SQL/BI usage and do not benefit from SQL warehouse features (query result cache, workload management). Manual daily teardown/recreation loses saved state (query history, cached results) and is fragile.

questions.q: A security team wants to be paged whenever the count of failed logins in the last hour exceeds 100. They already have a Databricks SQL query that returns that count. What is the standard native Databricks SQL feature to trigger a notification when the value crosses that threshold?
choices: Configure an ACL on the underlying Delta table with a maximum-row policy.
Create a Databricks SQL Alert on the query with a condition such as `count > 100` and a notification destination.
Wrap the query inside a Delta Live Tables pipeline with an `EXPECT` clause.
Enable Change Data Feed on the query result set and stream it into Slack.
questions.explanation: Databricks SQL Alerts are designed exactly for this: attach an alert to a saved query, set a comparison against a numeric column (for example `count > 100`), pick a refresh schedule, and add notification destinations (email, Slack, PagerDuty via webhooks). Table ACLs govern access, not thresholds. DLT `EXPECT` is a data-quality gate on pipeline rows, not an operational alert. Change Data Feed emits row-level changes on a table, which is unrelated to alerting on query results.

questions.q: An analyst is loading a nightly `customer_updates` table into a target `customers` Delta table. Rows may match an existing customer (needs update), be new (needs insert), or be unchanged. The load must be idempotent so re-running the same file does not create duplicates. Which SQL statement is the correct choice?
choices: INSERT INTO customers SELECT * FROM customer_updates;
COPY INTO customers FROM 'customer_updates';
MERGE INTO customers t USING customer_updates s ON t.id = s.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
REPLACE INTO customers SELECT * FROM customer_updates;
questions.explanation: `MERGE INTO` is the canonical upsert on Delta Lake: matched rows are updated in place and unmatched rows are inserted in a single transactional statement, and re-running with the same input is idempotent because the same `ON` predicate re-matches the same rows. A plain `INSERT` would duplicate rows on re-run. `COPY INTO` is an idempotent file-loading command but only inserts new files — it cannot update existing rows. Databricks SQL does not have a `REPLACE INTO` statement for row-level upserts.

questions.q: The analytics team needs the median customer order value. They know that `AVG()` is influenced by outliers and want the exact 50th percentile. Which Databricks SQL expression returns the median?
choices: SELECT AVG(order_value) FROM orders;
SELECT MID(order_value) FROM orders;
SELECT MEAN(order_value) FROM orders;
SELECT PERCENTILE(order_value, 0.5) FROM orders;
questions.explanation: `PERCENTILE(col, 0.5)` (or the newer `MEDIAN(col)` alias) returns the exact 50th percentile. `AVG()` and `MEAN()` return the arithmetic mean, which is pulled by outliers and is not the median. `MID()` is a substring function in some SQL dialects, not a statistical aggregate. For very large tables where a small approximation error is acceptable, `PERCENTILE_APPROX()` is often used instead for performance.

nodes.title: Part 3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Part 3. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: A Databricks SQL dashboard needs to display up-to-date figures every 15 minutes during business hours without requiring anyone to click Refresh. Which built-in configuration provides this?
flashcards.back: Databricks SQL dashboards support native scheduled refresh: pick an interval, pick the target warehouse, optionally list subscribers, and the platform re-runs the underlying queries and updates the dashboard. Structured Streaming outputs data to sinks, not dashboards. `VACUUM` retention has nothing to do with dashboard freshness — it only controls when tombstoned files can be physically deleted. A cron-driven notebook is a manual workaround that misses out on dashboard subscription, freshness metadata, and warehouse-level auto-scaling.

flashcards.front: An analyst has written a SELECT that aggregates order totals per region and wants to persist the result as a queryable, managed Delta table so BI users can reuse it. Which single Databricks SQL statement achieves this in one step?
flashcards.back: `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` (CTAS) creates a new managed Delta table whose schema and initial data both come from the query in one step. `COPY INTO` loads files into an existing table and cannot take an inline query as source. `INSERT OVERWRITE` and `UPDATE` both assume the target table already exists — they cannot create it. Once the table exists, refreshes can be handled with `INSERT OVERWRITE` or `MERGE` on a schedule.

flashcards.front: A table `orders(items ARRAY<INT>)` stores the list of item ids per order. The analyst wants a new column with each order's item ids doubled (for a promo simulation) — element-wise, without exploding the array. Which Databricks SQL expression does this?
flashcards.back: `transform(array, lambda)` is the higher-order function that applies the lambda to every element of an array and returns a new array of the same length. `explode` would turn the array into multiple rows, changing the row shape. `collect_list(items * 2)` is not valid because `items * 2` on an array is undefined and `collect_list` is a row-collapsing aggregate. `map(array, lambda)` is not a valid Databricks SQL function — `map` in SQL constructs a map (key/value) literal instead.

flashcards.front: An analyst has run a query that returns count of failed_logins by hour and wants to display it as a bar chart on a Databricks SQL dashboard, so operations can see spikes at a glance. What is the standard workflow in Databricks SQL?
flashcards.back: The standard workflow in Databricks SQL is to attach one or more Visualizations (Table, Bar, Line, Counter, Pivot, Map, etc.) to a saved query, configure X/Y and colour, and then add the visualization tile to a dashboard. Photon is a query-execution engine and does not create charts. Catalog Explorer's histogram is only a quick profiling view of a single column and cannot be embedded into a dashboard. Exporting to CSV and using an external BI tool is possible but bypasses Databricks SQL's native visualization + dashboarding path.

questions.q: A Databricks SQL dashboard needs to display up-to-date figures every 15 minutes during business hours without requiring anyone to click Refresh. Which built-in configuration provides this?
choices: Set a scheduled refresh on the dashboard, tied to an available SQL warehouse.
Create a Structured Streaming job that writes the dashboard HTML to DBFS.
Lower the Delta table's `VACUUM` retention to 15 minutes.
Attach a cron notebook that repeatedly calls `dbutils.notebook.run` on the dashboard path.
questions.explanation: Databricks SQL dashboards support native scheduled refresh: pick an interval, pick the target warehouse, optionally list subscribers, and the platform re-runs the underlying queries and updates the dashboard. Structured Streaming outputs data to sinks, not dashboards. `VACUUM` retention has nothing to do with dashboard freshness — it only controls when tombstoned files can be physically deleted. A cron-driven notebook is a manual workaround that misses out on dashboard subscription, freshness metadata, and warehouse-level auto-scaling.

questions.q: An analyst has written a SELECT that aggregates order totals per region and wants to persist the result as a queryable, managed Delta table so BI users can reuse it. Which single Databricks SQL statement achieves this in one step?
choices: COPY INTO region_totals FROM (SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region);
CREATE TABLE region_totals AS SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY region;
INSERT OVERWRITE region_totals SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region;
UPDATE region_totals SET total = (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE orders.region = region_totals.region);
questions.explanation: `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` (CTAS) creates a new managed Delta table whose schema and initial data both come from the query in one step. `COPY INTO` loads files into an existing table and cannot take an inline query as source. `INSERT OVERWRITE` and `UPDATE` both assume the target table already exists — they cannot create it. Once the table exists, refreshes can be handled with `INSERT OVERWRITE` or `MERGE` on a schedule.

questions.q: A table `orders(items ARRAY<INT>)` stores the list of item ids per order. The analyst wants a new column with each order's item ids doubled (for a promo simulation) — element-wise, without exploding the array. Which Databricks SQL expression does this?
choices: SELECT explode(items) * 2 AS doubled FROM orders;
SELECT collect_list(items * 2) AS doubled FROM orders;
SELECT transform(items, x -> x * 2) AS doubled FROM orders;
SELECT map(items, x -> x * 2) AS doubled FROM orders;
questions.explanation: `transform(array, lambda)` is the higher-order function that applies the lambda to every element of an array and returns a new array of the same length. `explode` would turn the array into multiple rows, changing the row shape. `collect_list(items * 2)` is not valid because `items * 2` on an array is undefined and `collect_list` is a row-collapsing aggregate. `map(array, lambda)` is not a valid Databricks SQL function — `map` in SQL constructs a map (key/value) literal instead.

questions.q: An analyst has run a query that returns count of failed_logins by hour and wants to display it as a bar chart on a Databricks SQL dashboard, so operations can see spikes at a glance. What is the standard workflow in Databricks SQL?
choices: Export the result to CSV, load it into Power BI Desktop, then embed the Power BI iframe in a Databricks widget.
Enable Photon on the warehouse, which auto-generates a bar-chart tab in the query result panel.
Write the result to a Delta table and rely on the built-in table-viewer histogram in Catalog Explorer.
In the query editor, add a Visualization of type Bar to the query, configure the axes, then add the visualization to the target dashboard.
questions.explanation: The standard workflow in Databricks SQL is to attach one or more Visualizations (Table, Bar, Line, Counter, Pivot, Map, etc.) to a saved query, configure X/Y and colour, and then add the visualization tile to a dashboard. Photon is a query-execution engine and does not create charts. Catalog Explorer's histogram is only a quick profiling view of a single column and cannot be embedded into a dashboard. Exporting to CSV and using an external BI tool is possible but bypasses Databricks SQL's native visualization + dashboarding path.
